title: 1 Chronicles 9:35–44
context: This unit repeats, with small differences, the genealogy of the Gibeonite family and Saul’s line from 8:29–38, and it leads directly into chapter 10, where Saul and his sons die on Mount Gilboa. Some spellings differ from chapter 8 (for example, Tarea in 8:35 and Tahrea in 9:41, Jehoaddah in 8:36 and Jarah in 9:42), and this version names Jeiel as the father of Gibeon (9:35) and includes Ner among his sons (9:36). The list ends with Azel’s six sons (9:44) and does not repeat 8:39–40. The text does not explain why the genealogy is repeated; it may serve to introduce Saul before chapter 10, but that is an inference. The identifications of Eshbaal and Merib-baal with the Ishbosheth and Mephibosheth of 2 Samuel are probable but not stated in Chronicles. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: it sets the stage for the end of Saul’s reign and the rise of David.

verses.text: Jeiel the father of Gibeon, whose wife’s name was Maacah, lived in Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeiel the father of Gibeon, whose wife was Maacah, lived in Gibeon. Arminian readers note that the genealogy of 8:29–38 is repeated here with small differences, including the name Jeiel. The repetition brings Saul’s family back into view just before his death in chapter 10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the repetition and its placement before chapter 10. The Chronicler does not explain why the list appears twice, and proposed reasons are inferences. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of a transition from the genealogies to the story of Israel’s kings.

verses.text: His firstborn son was Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab,
verses.arminianNotes: Abdon the firstborn, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab are named. Arminian readers note that this list includes Ner, who does not appear in 8:30. They record the difference plainly and read the verse as part of the family record that leads to Saul.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the inclusion of Ner and do not force agreement with chapter 8. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and affirm the trustworthiness of the record without requiring every parallel list to match exactly.

verses.arminianNotes: Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth complete the brothers. Arminian readers note that Zechariah here corresponds to Zecher in 8:31, a variation in the form of the name. The family remains the same despite the difference in spelling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the variant form calmly as common in ancient lists. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and agree that spelling differences between parallel lists raise no doctrinal question.

verses.text: Mikloth became the father of Shimeam. They also lived with their relatives in Jerusalem, near their relatives.
verses.arminianNotes: Mikloth fathers Shimeam, and the family lives with relatives in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the repeated link between this Gibeonite family and Jerusalem, as in 8:32, where the name appears as Shimeah. Benjamin’s ties to the holy city are again highlighted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the family’s presence in Jerusalem and the minor variant from 8:32. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting Saul’s wider family with the city of God’s house, a theme that matters for the restored community.

verses.text: Ner became the father of Kish. Kish became the father of Saul. Saul became the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
verses.arminianNotes: Ner fathers Kish, Kish fathers Saul, and Saul’s sons are Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. Arminian readers note that three of these sons will die with Saul at Gilboa (10:2). The list prepares the reader for the tragedy that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list setting the stage for chapter 10. Eshbaal is often identified with Ishbosheth (2 Samuel 2:8), though Chronicles does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Saul’s genealogy at the threshold of his fall, without speculating about the different lists in 1 Samuel.

verses.text: The son of Jonathan was Merib-baal. Merib-baal became the father of Micah.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan’s son is Merib-baal, the father of Micah. Arminian readers note that Merib-baal is often identified with Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4; 9:12), though Chronicles does not state it. Jonathan’s line continues even as Saul’s reign is about to end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification as probable and see in Jonathan’s surviving line a reminder of David’s covenant kindness to Jonathan’s house (2 Samuel 9:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing Jonathan’s family beyond the fall of Saul.

verses.text: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Micah’s sons are Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. Arminian readers note the minor variation from Tarea in 8:35. The repeated genealogy shows that Jonathan’s descendants continued for generations, and they read it as a record of family survival.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity and the small variant in spelling. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the repeated genealogy and see in it the long survival of Jonathan’s line, recorded plainly by the Chronicler.

verses.text: Ahaz became the father of Jarah. Jarah became the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri became the father of Moza.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz fathers Jarah, whose sons include Zimri, the father of Moza. Arminian readers note that 8:36 reads Jehoaddah for Jarah. They record the difference without harmonizing and read the verse as part of the continuing family record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the variant and do not force agreement. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and affirm that the faithful preservation of these lists does not depend on harmonizing every form of a name.

verses.text: Moza became the father of Binea, Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, and Azel his son.
verses.arminianNotes: Moza fathers Binea, followed by Rephaiah, Eleasah, and Azel. Arminian readers note the variation from Raphah in 8:37 and the continuing father-to-son pattern. The line moves steadily forward through generations that receive no other mention in Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity and the variant form. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a link in the chain of Jonathan’s descendants and see in it God’s preservation of a family long after the events of Saul’s reign.

verses.text: Azel had six sons, whose names are Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. These were the sons of Azel.
verses.arminianNotes: Azel’s six sons close the list, matching 8:38. Arminian readers note that this version stops here, without the further generations of 8:39–40. The genealogies end, and the narrative of Saul’s last battle begins in the next chapter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the list ends at this point and leads directly into chapter 10, where the story of David’s kingdom begins with the fall of Saul. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the end of the genealogies and the threshold of the Chronicler’s narrative of the kings.
